title: The Cameronians: no harm to the will's freedom
source_text: LXI. Ex parte vero voluntatis, quanquam quae descripta est gratiae operatio, necessario ejus consensum eliciat, nullatenus tamen illi libertatem adimit. Nec enim voluntatem movet, & determinat, nisi per intellectus practici judicium. Sed ex virorum illorum doctorum sententia, necessitas & determinatio actuum voluntatis, quae ex mentis practicae judicio oritur, non obstat quominus libere a voluntate procedant: quandoquidem libertas voluntatis non opponitur cuivis necessitati, sed illi tantum, quae est a vi externa, a materia, vel a sensu. Quae latius diducta videre est apud Mosen Amyraldum tractatu de libero arbitrio, praecipue Sectione quarta. Et similiter in libro posthumo Josuae Placei de eodem argumento.
pass_a_gloss: LXI. But on the part of the will, although the operation of grace that has been described necessarily elicits its consent, yet it in no way takes away its freedom. For it does not move & determine the will, except through the judgment of the practical intellect. But in the opinion of those learned men, the necessity & determination of the acts of the will, which arises from the practical judgment of the mind, does not prevent their proceeding freely from the will: since freedom of the will is not opposed to every necessity, but only to that which is from external force, from matter, or from sense. Which may be seen set out more broadly in Moses Amyraldus' treatise on free will, especially Section four. And similarly in the posthumous book of Josua Placeus on the same subject.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXI. As for the will, the working of grace described above does necessarily draw out its consent, yet it in no way takes its freedom away, since it moves and determines the will only through the judgment of the practical intellect.

In these learned men's view, the necessity and determination of the will's acts that come from the mind's practical judgment do not stop those acts from proceeding freely from the will. The will's freedom is not opposed to every necessity, only to necessity that comes from outside force, from matter or from the senses.
This is argued more fully in Moses Amyraldus' treatise on free will, especially section 4, and likewise in Josua Placeus' posthumous book on the same subject.
